sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
Global equity markets registered a broadly constructive August 2026, with US technology stocks staging their strongest August performance since 2021 and the S&P 500 marking its fifth consecutive monthly gain. Risk appetite held up despite persistent geopolitical friction in the Middle East, as periodic US military strikes on Iranian positions in and around the Strait of Hormuz injected volatility — particularly toward month-end — without derailing the broader bull market narrative.

The divergence across regions was meaningful: the Nasdaq Composite surged **+3.5%** and the S&P 500 advanced **+2.5%**, while Europe was mixed and APAC faced more challenging conditions. Japan's Nikkei 225 declined sharply amid yen appreciation and risk-off flows tied to Middle East tensions, while China's Shanghai Composite and Hong Kong's Hang Seng held broadly rangebound. Continental European markets split, with Germany's export-oriented DAX outperforming and France's CAC 40 slipping.

Overall, August reinforced the dominance of AI-driven growth narratives in setting the tone for global equity sentiment, even as central bank policy uncertainty and geopolitical risk factors capped upside in rate-sensitive and commodity-importing markets.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes: US-Iran Military Escalation Roils Energy Markets -- The defining macro shock of August arrived on the final trading day of the month, when US forces struck Iranian rocket launcher positions along the Strait of Hormuz — the first military action in roughly a month — sending oil prices surging and triggering a late-session selloff across equity markets. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than **400 points** and the S&P 500 declined **0.3%** on August 31 alone, paring what had been a constructive month-end rally. Brent crude had already breached **$94/bbl** in the week of August 24 on Trump administration threats of secondary sanctions against Iranian oil trading partners, before settling near **$90.55/bbl** by August 28 ahead of the final escalation. Strategically, the conflict's disruption of roughly 20 million barrels per day of crude and **30%** of global seaborne hydrocarbons transiting the Strait represents a persistent tail risk to global energy supply chains, with any further military escalation capable of repricing energy markets materially higher.

Jackson Hole Hawkish Pivot Renews Rate-Hike Fears -- With no FOMC meeting scheduled for August, markets pivoted to the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium as the key monetary policy signpost, and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's public remarks highlighted persistent inflation concerns — with US CPI running above the **2%** target for more than five consecutive years. The hawkish tone amplified speculation of a September rate increase. A 9–3 FOMC vote in July to hold the federal funds rate at **3.50%–3.75%** had already revealed growing internal dissent, with three regional presidents advocating for an immediate hike. By early August, Fed funds futures implied a nearly **55%** probability of a September quarter-point increase, reshaping the risk calculus across duration assets, growth equities, and emerging markets. The 2-year Treasury yield climbed sharply from **4.17%** in mid-August to **4.34%** by month-end, with the 10-year moving from **4.68%** to **4.73%**, collectively signaling that the market is no longer pricing in the next Fed move as a cut.

Copper's Record-Breaking Supply Squeeze -- Industrial metals captured the attention of commodity markets as copper futures struck a record high of **$6.70/lb** on August 25, before pulling back to **$6.50/lb** by month-end. The rally was driven by acute supply-side pressures: top global producer Chile reported a **9.4%** year-on-year decline in copper output in July amid mine disruptions, compounding a structural supply deficit against the backdrop of surging green energy and AI data-center infrastructure demand. S&P Global's market outlook flagged that supply shortages are likely to persist through 2026 and into 2027, providing a structural floor under prices even as macroeconomic headwinds from elevated US rates and slowing Chinese industrial activity applied short-term pressure. The record copper print underscores the commodity's growing role as a bellwether for the global energy transition capex cycle and lends further credence to the electrification supercycle thesis that has underpinned base-metals bulls for the past two years.

AI Mega-Cycle Powers Nasdaq's Best August Since 2021 -- The singular force animating US equity risk appetite through August was the continued acceleration of the artificial intelligence investment mega-cycle, which drove the Nasdaq-100 to a gain of **+4.2%** for the month — its best August performance since 2021 — while the Nasdaq Composite climbed **+3.5%** to close at **26,370.89**, snapping two consecutive months of losses. Mega-cap technology names continued to expand earnings multiples on the back of strong AI-linked revenue growth and robust cloud infrastructure spending, while semiconductor stocks and software platforms tied to large language model deployment were consistent outperformers. The S&P 500's **+2.5%** gain to **7,686.14** masked considerable dispersion underneath, with technology and communication services contributing the bulk of index-level returns while energy, utilities, and financials lagged amid rising rate expectations. Notably, the Nasdaq's outsized August gain came despite a deteriorating rate backdrop — a sign that AI enthusiasm is presently capable of overriding the conventional inverse relationship between long-duration growth equities and Treasury yields.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities advanced in August, with the S&P 500 rising **+2.5%** to close at **7,686.14**, the Nasdaq Composite gaining **+3.5%** to **26,370.89**, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average posting a more modest **+1.0%** advance to **53,185.90**. The month marked the fifth consecutive monthly gain for the Dow and snapped two consecutive months of losses for the Nasdaq-100, which surged **+4.2%** — its strongest August showing since 2021.

The primary driver was the ongoing AI investment cycle, which continued to generate outsized earnings expectations for mega-cap technology companies. Cloud infrastructure spending, semiconductor demand, and software monetization of AI capabilities provided the fundamental underpinning for multiple expansion in the tech-heavy indices. At the same time, the Nasdaq-100's gains came despite rising rate-hike probability, underscoring the degree to which AI enthusiasm is capable of overriding the conventional inverse relationship between long-duration growth equities and interest rate expectations.

The month ended on a sobering note as markets absorbed the August 31 US military strikes against Iranian positions in the Strait of Hormuz. The S&P 500 shed **0.3%** and the Dow fell over **400 points** on that session alone, paring some of the month's gains. Nevertheless, the dip-buying reflex remains intact, and the breadth of the August rally — anchored by technology — suggests institutional investors remain net constructive on the US equity outlook into year-end.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity performance was mixed in August, with divergence across major bourses reflecting idiosyncratic domestic factors layered onto a common backdrop of Middle East geopolitical risk and Fed policy uncertainty. Germany's DAX outperformed, rising **+1.66%** for the month as industrial capex optimism, AI infrastructure investment flows, and broadly supportive ECB communication underpinned German blue-chip sentiment. By contrast, France's CAC 40 declined **-0.98%** amid domestic political headwinds and weaker consumer confidence data, while the UK's FTSE 100 finished almost unchanged at **+0.07%** — effectively flat on the month.

Energy stocks provided a tailwind across the continent as Brent crude's August surge — particularly in the second half of the month as Middle East tensions intensified — boosted the earnings outlooks for integrated energy majors. However, rate-sensitive sectors including real estate, utilities, and financials faced headwinds as expectations for European Central Bank rate cuts were modestly pushed out in sympathy with the global shift in fixed income pricing driven by Jackson Hole.

The region's equity tape continues to trade at a meaningful valuation discount to US peers, a gap that value-oriented institutional investors have noted but that has yet to catalyze a sustained rotation. Until European earnings growth can demonstrate clearer independence from the global growth cycle and fiscal policy clarity improves — particularly in France and Italy — the discount appears likely to persist heading into the autumn reporting season.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian equity markets faced more challenging conditions in August, with Japan's Nikkei 225 underperforming notably amid yen appreciation and geopolitical risk-off pressure. The index closed the month at **66,311.93**, representing an approximate decline of **-4%** to **-5%** from late-July levels, as seasonal USD/JPY weakness compressed the earnings outlook for export-oriented corporates including Toyota, Sony, and leading semiconductor manufacturers. The Nikkei touched an intra-month high near **69,220** on August 17 before the late-month risk-off wave driven by Iran escalation and hawkish Fed commentary erased those gains.

China's Shanghai Composite held its ground more constructively, ending August at **3,986.30** — roughly flat to marginally positive for the month — supported by incremental domestic stimulus signals and signs of tentative stabilization in the property sector. The Hang Seng Index closed at **25,566.99**, similarly rangebound as investors awaited more decisive fiscal policy signals from Beijing before committing capital to a more substantive recovery trade.

The APAC divergence between Japan's risk-off pressure and China's tentative stabilization underscores the region's structural heterogeneity. Near-term catalysts for a sustained Japanese equity re-rating remain tied to BOJ policy trajectory and yen direction, while Chinese equities continue to require confirmation of the fiscal stimulus pipeline materializing in hard economic data before a sustained re-rating of valuations appears warranted.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar consolidated modestly in August, with the DXY Index edging higher by **+0.45%** to close near **100.23** — having started the month around **99.78** — supported by the market's reassessment of Fed policy toward a higher-for-longer and potentially hike-biased stance following Jackson Hole. The move was restrained relative to the magnitude of the rate repricing, suggesting residual structural headwinds for the dollar from twin deficit dynamics and ongoing geopolitical de-dollarization trends.

EUR/USD touched a three-month high of **1.1710** in mid-August before pulling back toward **1.1600** at month-end as dollar demand firmed ahead of the anticipated September FOMC decision. GBP/USD tracked its historical seasonal pattern of August underperformance — consistent with average returns of approximately **-0.5%** since 1971 — with sterling facing additional pressure from UK domestic growth concerns and energy import cost inflation driven by the Middle East supply disruption. USD/JPY declined in line with historical August seasonality, reflecting yen repatriation flows and modest BOJ rate expectations.

The FX backdrop heading into September is asymmetric: a Fed rate hike would reinforce dollar strength and pressure emerging-market currencies, while a hold would likely see EUR/USD recover toward the **1.1700–1.1750** range. Oil-correlated currencies — notably the Canadian dollar and Norwegian krone — benefited from crude's late-August surge, providing a partial offset to the broad risk-off dollar demand triggered by the Iran strikes on the final trading day.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Commodities delivered a bifurcated performance in August, with energy and industrial metals advancing strongly while precious metals faced sharp late-month volatility. Brent crude moved in a wide range, surging to **$94/bbl** in the week of August 24 as Trump administration threats of secondary sanctions on Iranian oil trading partners stoked supply-disruption fears, before settling near **$90.55/bbl** on August 28 and spiking again on August 31 following US military strikes. WTI crude similarly advanced, trading near **$87/bbl** in late August — a level consistent with the supply-tightening narrative driven by the Strait of Hormuz conflict.

Copper was the standout performer in industrial metals, printing a record high of **$6.70/lb** on August 25 before pulling back to **$6.50/lb** by month-end amid macroeconomic headwinds. The rally reflected acute supply-side pressure, with top producer Chile reporting a **9.4%** year-on-year output decline in July, layered onto structural demand growth from green energy and AI data-center infrastructure. Gold closed August at **$4,431.82/oz**, retreating sharply from the August 25 high of **$4,598/oz** as the metal sold off counterintuitively on the Iran strikes amid dollar strength and profit-taking; the monthly percentage change relative to July's close remains.

The commodity complex heading into September presents a dual narrative: structurally tight supply in copper and energy transition metals supports a bullish medium-term thesis, while the Iran conflict introduces near-term energy price volatility capable of simultaneously boosting oil-linked revenues and compressing industrial margins through higher input costs globally.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
US Treasury markets repriced materially in August as Jackson Hole communications from Fed Chair Warsh reinforced the possibility of a September rate hike and cast doubt on the previously consensus view that the next Fed move would be a cut. The 10-year Treasury yield rose from **4.68%** in mid-August to **4.73%** by month-end, while the 2-year yield climbed more sharply from **4.17%** to **4.34%**, generating a modest steepening of the yield curve to a positive **39 basis-point** spread between 10s and 2s.

The Fed maintained its federal funds target range at **3.50%–3.75%** at the July FOMC — the fifth consecutive hold of 2026 — though three dissenting votes for an immediate rate increase underscored the building hawkish pressure within the Committee. With inflation running above the **2%** target for over five consecutive years, markets now attach a nearly **55%** probability to a 25 basis-point hike at the September 16 meeting, a shift that has driven meaningful repricing across the rates curve and spread products.

The fixed income outlook into the autumn is fraught with binary risk. A September hike would push the 2-year yield toward the **4.50%–4.60%** range and the 10-year closer to **4.90%–5.00%**, creating renewed pressure on rate-sensitive equities and widening credit spreads. Conversely, a hold accompanied by dovish forward guidance could trigger a significant bond rally. Against this backdrop, duration management and positioning around the September FOMC outcome represent the critical fixed income risk variables for portfolio allocators through year-end.
